<description>
{
 "summary": "Updates 1P1C package construction in TxDownloadManagerImpl to check if candidate orphan transactions are already in the mempool. If a candidate child exists in the mempool, it is erased from the orphanage and skipped. This preserves the invariant that package evaluation never receives an already-admitted child, retaining the Assume(false) assertion for MEMPOOL_ENTRY in net_processing.",
 "problem": "Orphan transactions that enter the mempool through non-peer mechanisms such as RPC submission are not automatically evicted from the orphanage. When a reconsiderable parent subsequently arrives from a peer, Find1P1CPackage could select that orphan as a package child, resulting in a MEMPOOL_ENTRY acceptance result that triggers an Assume(false) assertion failure in debug builds.",
 "evidence": [
  "PR description: 'An orphan that enters the mempool other than through peer relay (e.g. by RPC) stays in the orphanage, so Find1P1CPackage can pick it as the child of a reconsiderable parent, and package evaluation then reports it as MEMPOOL_ENTRY, which hits Assume(false).'",
  "The added functional test (test_orphan_in_mempool) reproduces the exact issue: an orphan submitted via submitpackage enters the mempool while remaining in the orphanage, triggering the code path upon receiving the reconsiderable parent."
 ],

<category name="p2p" title="P2P">
## Covers

Everything between this node and other nodes: connection management and
peer selection, address management, the message protocol and its
transport (including the encrypted v2 transport), block and transaction
relay including compact blocks, headers sync, transaction request and
orphan handling, network-level DoS protections, and the Tor, I2P, and
CJDNS integrations. The P2P and Private Broadcast labels are a strong
prior.

Not p2p: what the node does with a block or transaction once received
(validation, mempool); RPCs that merely report peer state (rpc).

## What matters here

Resistance to attack first: eclipse and partition resistance, DoS
resistance in message handling and resource accounting, and privacy of
transaction origin. Then relay correctness and liveness: blocks and
transactions propagate reliably and quickly, and nothing gets stuck.
Then interoperability with the rest of the network and with new
protocol features (BIPs) that other software depends on. Then bandwidth
and resource use, which node operators feel. Then connectivity across
network types and platforms.

Protocol changes with a specification and other implementations
waiting rank higher than local optimizations. Refactors count when they
retire a known hazard in message handling.
